title: The Disclosure Conditions Hypothesis: Youth-Facing Sextortion Response Resources and the Anticipated Manageability of Seeking Help
content: Research with young people who experienced sextortion or image-based sexual abuse as minors reports nondisclosure alongside embarrassment, anticipated blame, and fear of consequences. A public response resource can communicate an institution’s position before any personal contact occurs, yet what such a resource must make explicit for seeking help to appear manageable remains an open question. This article advances the disclosure conditions hypothesis: a young person’s anticipatory appraisal of seeking help is shaped in part by seven conditions that a youth-facing sextortion response resource makes available, three reception-related (reachability, decodability, and credibility) and four disclosure-supportive (absolution, relational scaffolding, pathway coherence, and consequence transparency). The least supported applicable condition constrains that appraisal more than the total amount of supportive content. It is derived from documentary research, appraisal and help-seeking theory, disclosure research, institutional betrayal and courage, and communication appraisal. Six component hypotheses are stated, each with the evidence it requires and the results that would count against it. A document-level coding procedure, a hypothetical worked comparison, and a staged test plan keep separate what a resource says, how a young person experiences it, and what support is delivered. No data are reported; the conditions and coding rules remain provisional.
